It stays inactive on the same words in phrase-internal or filler uses - 'the', 'is', 'and', bare subject/object relatives ('which', 'who', 'whom'), degree 'so', 'how many', 'how to', verb-adjunct 'for' ('used for', 'paid for') and an ordinary sentence full stop - and its strength does not change when only the following content changes.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Mount Rainier is an active stratovolcano in Washington State, and its summit rises more than four thousand metres above sea level. The mountain carries the largest glacier system in the contiguous United States, and meltwater from these glaciers feeds several major rivers. Geologists have mapped the deposits left by lahars, mudflows of volcanic debris able to travel dozens of kilometres down river valleys. Such flows are especially dangerous because they can arrive with little warning, long after an eruption has ended. The most recent major lahar occurred about five hundred years ago, and evidence of it survives in soil layers beneath the surrounding lowland forests. Researchers studying the volcano's history have drilled cores into lake sediments to reconstruct the timing of past eruptions. By counting ash layers and dating organic material trapped between them, they can estimate how often the mountain has erupted during the past ten thousand years. The record suggests large eruptions occur roughly every few centuries, though the intervals are irregular. A similar pattern appears at Mount Hood and Mount Shasta, though the spacing of eruptions varies considerably. The volcano is considered among the most dangerous in the country, largely because of the number of people living near its flanks. Monitoring the volcano involves a network of seismometers, GPS receivers, and gas sensors, and these instruments transmit measurements to a central observatory. Scientists track changes in the shape of the summit and in the rate of small earthquakes. These signals can indicate movement of magma beneath the surface, although they rarely lead to an eruption. Emergency planners rely on the hazard maps derived from this research when they approve new construction. The maps show the likely paths of future lahars and the areas likely to be buried by ash. Public education campaigns encourage residents to prepare an emergency kit and to learn evacuation routes. The conditions under which the observatory issues a formal alert are reviewed every year. Officials also practice communication drills with local radio stations and hospitals, and a full-scale exercise takes place each spring. The results are published in an annual report available to the public. Visitors to the national park receive leaflets explaining the volcanic hazards and the steps to take during an emergency. Rangers remind hikers to check the weather and to carry enough water, even on short walks above the tree line.
